svg.text: worth-fees — from a published CMS release to one priced answer
What enters at each stage, what leaves it, and what is refused. Every amount arrives with the arithmetic that produced it and the hash of every file it was read from.
runs once per release · offline afterwards
Strip what must not be kept
a refusal beats a wrong number
two per release, one per basis
Written on load, not on read
the read is a lookup, not a sum
so stored rows cannot go stale
the date picks the release, so
a Q1 claim never gets Q3 rates
a schedule figure, not a payment
the hash of every file involved
Or a refusal, with a reason
Quarterly release archives — the only upstream data source. CMS publishes the fee schedule four times a year as archives; each is
pinned here by its address and its hash, so the exact bytes in play are named before anything is read from them.
Three data files inside each archive — the relative value of every code (published twice, once per payment basis), the geographic
cost indices for every locality, and the crosswalk naming which counties each locality covers.
Download and verify — the archive's hash is compared against the pinned value before a single byte is parsed. A truncated download,
or a file quietly re-cut upstream, becomes a loud failure here rather than a subtly wrong dollar amount later.
Read and validate — every row is checked against CMS's own published totals. If the values being read do not add up to the sums CMS
printed alongside them, the file is not laid out the way it is expected to be, and ingestion stops instead of guessing.
Strip what must not be kept — the written descriptions of each code are copyrighted by the AMA. They are never read on the way in
and never written out, so neither the public repository nor the database can leak them. You cannot spill what you never held.
Refuse rather than guess — codes Medicare does not pay under this schedule, settings CMS marks unpayable, and modifiers that scale
the amount are all rejected. Every one of those, priced naively, returns a real-looking number. A refusal is a result; that is not.
Releases and their dates — one row per CMS publication, carrying the span of service dates it governs and when it was fetched. Two
clocks are kept apart: when the rate applied, and when you learned it. You need both to explain a number you published last year.
The provenance chain — every file the data passed through, with its hash, linked child to parent back to the original archive. This is
what lets a hostile reviewer re-download the source and re-hash it themselves instead of taking your word for the number.
Values for every code — roughly 19,226 rows per release: the physician-work, practice-expense and malpractice components, whether
the code is payable, its global period, and the payment-policy indicators. The indicators are stored but never priced from.
Geography — the 109 Medicare localities, each with its three cost indices, the counties it covers and the contractor that processes
claims there. The same procedure with the same components is priced 109 different ways; that spread is the point.
Conversion factors — dollars per unit of value, one per payment basis. Held apart from the codes because the two bases differ in this
number and in nothing else, so the components are stored once rather than duplicated to vary a single figure.
Every combination priced — code × locality × setting × payment basis, expanded and computed on load. Combinations with no payable
amount are left out entirely, so the stored table cannot hand back a price for a service that does not have one.
The size — roughly 8.4M rows per quarterly release, about 34M for a full CY2026 year, at an estimated 0.5–1 GB
per release. That is the price of trading a computation for a stored lookup, and it buys nothing the inputs did not already hold.
Written on load, not on read — the expansion runs once, when a release is loaded, and the result is indexed. A query then reads a
row that already exists rather than doing the arithmetic again, which is what makes a full-table scan across all codes cheap.
Rebuilt when a release lands — the whole set is re-derived from a single definition rather than edited in place, so the stored rows
cannot drift away from the formula that defines them. This is the guarantee the stored design has to earn back.
What is being priced — the procedure code, any modifiers, and whether the work happened in a facility or not. The setting matters
because the practice-expense component differs between the two, sometimes by more than fifty dollars.
Where and when — the Medicare locality, and the date the service actually happened. Not today's date: the rate that applies is the
one that was in force on the date of service, which is why the release a query resolves to is never simply the newest one.
On which basis — the standard rate, or the higher one paid to qualifying advanced-payment-model participants. CMS publishes both,
so a request for a price that does not say which one it means is an unanswered question rather than a default.
Resolved, then looked up — the date of service selects the release, and the rest of the query selects the row within it. A
first-quarter claim is never priced at third-quarter rates, and exactly one release is in force for any given date.
The allowed amount — the figure, in cents. It is what the schedule allows, not what anyone was paid: Medicare pays 80% of it, the
patient owes the rest, and further adjustments move it again. None of that is modelled, and treating this as a payment is a misuse.
The arithmetic — every multiplication and running total that produced the figure, at full precision, so it can be redone on paper by
someone who does not trust the system that produced it. No binary floating point touches the money at any stage.
The receipts — the hash of every file the number came from, chained back to the original CMS archive. This is the difference between
a number on a screen and an argument someone else can check without trusting you, which is the whole point of the package.
Or a refusal — when there is no payable amount, the answer is an explicit reason rather than a figure. Most ways of getting this wrong
produce a plausible number instead of an error, which is precisely what an explicit refusal is there to prevent.
Downstream — the allowed amount is the denominator for the complexity-matched expected payment in worth-complexity. It is an input
to that argument, not the output of this one: the question there is whether a payment was adequate for the work actually done.

Stage 4 is target state. Today those combinations are computed when queried rather than stored: the database holds the ~78,000 input rows and derives each amount on read. Materialising them is the change this diagram depicts.
No amount produced by this package has been checked against CMS. The claim today is that the arithmetic is reproducible, not that the number is right.

Scope: Medicare Physician Fee Schedule only — no OPPS, ASC, IPPS, anesthesia, clinical lab, DMEPOS, Part B drugs or commercial rates. Public CMS data throughout; no PHI, no payer or institution rates, no code descriptions.
